Munajat-e-Maqbool

Saturday

First manzil · supplications 1 to 54

Opening praise

In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

We praise You, O best of those in whom hope is placed and most generous of those from whom anything is sought, for teaching us Munajat-e-Maqbool, which brings nearness to Allah, and the supplications of the Messenger. Send perfect blessings upon him for as long as the west and east winds blow, and branches spring from their roots. Then we ask You for what we are about to recite. Ours is to ask, and Yours is to grant acceptance.

How to read

Read this opening invocation before each daily portion. Begin on Saturday, read one portion each day in order, and complete the cycle on Friday.

Swipe right to left to turn the page

In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

Supplication1

Good in both worlds

Our Lord, grant us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.

Original commentary 1

This is one of the most comprehensive supplications, which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, frequently recited. Consider its meaning: it teaches us to pray for success in both worlds.

Sources and notesSaturday · Prayer p. 9 · Quranic excerpt

Qur’an 2:201

Excerpt. Not applicable: Qur’anic text.

Sahih al-Bukhari 6389

Parallel only: Commentary: frequent Prophetic use of this prayer. Sahih: included by al-Bukhari in his Sahih. Anas identifies this as the Prophet’s most frequent supplication.

Supplication3

Forgiveness and relief from burdens

Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or make a mistake. Our Lord, do not lay upon us a burden like that which You laid upon those before us. Our Lord, do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear. Pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy on us. You are our Protector, so grant us victory over the disbelieving people.

Reading note

The original indicates a pause after 'Pardon us' and after 'Have mercy on us'.

Original commentary 3

The above supplication is a magnificent gift that came from the exalted Throne on the night of the Ascension. It asks: O Allah, do not place upon us a burden we cannot bear. These words should be on one's tongue morning and evening.

Sources and notesSaturday · Prayer p. 10 · Quranic excerpt

Qur’an 2:286

Excerpt. Not applicable: Qur’anic text.

Sahih Muslim 173

Parallel only: Commentary: the final verses of al-Baqarah given on the Night Journey. Sahih: included by Muslim in his Sahih. The primary text lists the final verses among three gifts given during the Night Journey.

Ahmad 21564

Parallel only: Commentary: the final verses from a treasure beneath the Throne. Shuʿayb al-Arnaut: sahih li-ghayrihi. The primary text describes the final verses as given from a treasure beneath the Throne.

The commentary’s Night Journey and Throne statements have the separate sources listed. Its morning-and-evening recommendation is devotional advice, not a timing established by those reports.

Supplication8

Faith and a righteous end

Our Lord, we heard a caller calling to faith: 'Believe in your Lord,' and we believed. Our Lord, forgive us our sins, wipe away our evil deeds, and cause us to die among the righteous.

Original commentary 8

This supplication asks: O Allah, forgive us our sins and remove our evil deeds. Above all, it asks that Allah grant us an end in the company of the righteous. A hadith states that for a person who recites 'O Allah, protect me from the Fire' three times each morning and evening, Hell itself will intercede, saying: O Allah, save this person from Hell. This supplication is a sign of a good ending.

Sources and notesSaturday · Prayer p. 12 · Quranic excerpt

Qur’an 3:193

Excerpt. Not applicable: Qur’anic text.

Jami al-Tirmidhi 2572

Parallel only: Commentary only: asking protection from the Fire three times and the Fire’s intercession. Darussalam: sahih. The report specifies three requests but no morning or evening timing.

Sunan Abi Dawud 5079

Parallel only: Comparison with the separate morning/evening report; does not verify the commentary’s combined claim. Al-Albani: daʿif. This report gives seven repetitions after Maghrib and Fajr, not three, and describes protection if one dies that night or day.

The printed qāf is a recitation annotation, not an additional word of the verse. The source commentary combines a threefold request with morning/evening timing. Tirmidhi 2572 supports the threefold request and intercession without that timing; the separate Abu Dawud 5079 report specifies seven after Maghrib and Fajr and is graded weak by al-Albani. The combined count-and-timing claim is not verified. The original printed page 12 contains the same claim, so it is inherited from the source commentary. The spelling of sayyi’atina also follows the original edition’s Indo-Pak form.

Supplication10

Adam and his wife’s prayer of repentance

Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we shall surely be among the losers.

Reading note

The original indicates a brief pause after 'we have wronged ourselves'.

This supplication was made by Adam, peace be upon him, and every Muslim should include it among their prayers. Through its blessing, sins are forgiven and Allah's mercy is obtained. Excerpt. Not applicable: Qur’anic text.

Supplication16

Forgiveness for parents and believers

Our Lord, forgive me, my parents and the believers on the Day when the reckoning is established.

Original source note 15 · on supplication 16

Every Muslim recites this supplication after the Tashahhud in prayer. It teaches us to ask forgiveness for ourselves, our parents and all Muslims, and to gather provision for the Hereafter. It is a tremendous supplication for parents. Scholars have written that reciting it often serves as atonement for shortcomings and neglect in fulfilling one's parents' rights.

Sources and notesSaturday · Prayer p. 16 · Quranic excerpt

Qur’an 14:41

Excerpt. Not applicable: Qur’anic text.

The commentary describes recitation after tashahhud as a universal practice, but does not establish a universal requirement. No specific hadith was verified for the claim that frequent recitation itself atones for neglect of parents’ rights. Prayer for parents does not by itself cancel outstanding duties to them.

Sources and notesSaturday · Prayer p. 17 · Quranic excerpt

Qur’an 18:10

Excerpt. Not applicable: Qur’anic text.

The first sentence of the original note 19 explains this prayer, but its ensuing Hijrah explanation belongs to number 18 (Qur’an 17:80). Number 19 is the prayer of the youths of the cave (Qur’an 18:10). Original printed page 15 already contains this conflation. The source note is therefore labelled as concerning both numbers 18 and 19; the cave prayer is not established here as the Prophet’s migration invocation.

Supplication43

The good sought by the Prophet

We ask You for the good which Your Prophet Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, asked of You.

Original commentary 43

This supplication sums up the prayers made by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, over twenty-three years. Its meaning is: O Allah, grant us all the good that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, asked of You.

Sources and notesSaturday · Prayer p. 26 · Hadith excerpt

Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 3521

Excerpt. Al-Tirmidhi: hasan gharīb; Darussalam edition: da‘if. This is the opening request after Allahumma; the report continues with refuge from evil. Al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan gharīb; the Darussalam edition grades it daʿif.

Hadith attribution is traceable, with disagreement in grading. The blessing on the Prophet is a devotional insertion. There is no unanimous sahih assessment among the cited authorities; the meaning also parallels the authenticated comprehensive prayer in Ibn Majah 3846. The note’s reference to twenty-three years is the author’s explanation of the prayer’s comprehensive meaning; it is not a twenty-three-year period stated in the cited hadith.

Supplication44

Forgiveness, good deeds and salvation

We ask You for the means of Your forgiveness, the deeds that fulfil Your command, safety from every sin, a share of every good, success in attaining Paradise, and deliverance from the Fire.

Original commentary 44

This supplication asks: O Allah, grant us the means of forgiveness and the ability to do deeds that bring salvation. It is an excellent means of obtaining Allah's mercy and forgiveness.

Sources and notesSaturday · Prayer p. 26 · Hadith variant; weak report

Al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak 1957

Variant: Most of the entry; the phrase mujibat amrik is not the wording in the inspected texts. Shu‘ayb al-Arna’ut, Takhrij Riyad al-Salihin 1493: chain contains Humayd al-A‘raj, reported abandoned/weak by named critics. Al-Hakim’s text reads aza’im maghfiratik wa munjiyat amrik; Riyad al-Salihin 1493 reads mujibat rahmatik. Both recensions include safety from sin, gain from good, Paradise and escape from the Fire.

Traceable to a weak Ibn Masʿud report. The book’s mujibat amrik is not supported by either wording in the cited hadith texts. Original printed page 21 also reads mujibat amrik, so this is inherited source wording, not an English-edition transcription error. This edition follows that source reading; its exact wording has not been authenticated.

Locator: Ahmad 17905; Tabarani 8369. Variant. Shu‘ayb al-Arna’ut: Ahmad 17905 has a sahih chain on Muslim’s conditions. Ahmad has singular dhanbi; the Tabarani text has plural dhunubi with wa before khata’i. The entry has the plural with apposition instead of that conjunction.

Supplication52

Religion, worldly life and the Hereafter

O Allah, put right for me my religion, which safeguards my affairs. Put right for me my worldly life, in which is my livelihood. Put right for me my Hereafter, to which I must return. Make life an increase for me in every good, and make death a relief for me from every evil.

Original commentary 52

This supplication asks for one's religion and worldly life to be safeguarded, one's Hereafter to be put right, goodness in every moment of life, and protection from every evil and trial at the time of death. It also reminds us of the purpose of life: O Allah, make every moment of our lives a means of increasing our good deeds. Every single word of this supplication is a guarantee of our well-being in this world and the Hereafter.

Sources and notesSaturday · Prayer p. 29 · Hadith exact

Sahih Muslim 2720

Exact. Sahih: included by Muslim in his Sahih. The complete Arabic matches the Abu Hurayrah report.

Full supplication in Sahih Muslim; no unsupported additions found. The commentary’s language of a guarantee is devotional praise of the prayer’s comprehensive requests, not an explicit unconditional reward found in Muslim 2720.

Supplication54

Comprehensive protection from spiritual and worldly harms

O Allah, I seek refuge in You from helplessness, laziness, cowardice, decrepit old age, debt and sin; from the punishment of the Fire and the trial of the Fire; from the trial of the grave and the punishment of the grave; from the evil trial of wealth and the evil trial of poverty; from the evil trial of the false Messiah; and from the trials of life and death;

from hardness of heart, heedlessness, poverty, humiliation, destitution, unbelief, wickedness, dissension, seeking praise and showing off; from deafness, loss of speech, madness, leprosy and grievous illnesses; from the burden of debt, anxiety, sorrow, miserliness and being overpowered by others; from being reduced to the feeblest stage of old age, the trials of this world, knowledge that does not benefit, a heart that does not humble itself, a soul that is never satisfied, and a prayer that is not answered.

Original commentary 54

In this supplication, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, mentions forty or fifty things from which refuge is sought, such as laziness, cowardice, debt, the punishment of the grave, disbelief, poverty, sin, every kind of illness, anxiety and so on. In this hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has expressed each and every one of our needs. These supplications show that no one besides the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, could teach in this way.

Sources and notesSaturday · Prayer p. 30 · Composite of hadith excerpts

Sahih Muslim 2722

Component: Helplessness, laziness, cowardice, old age; final four requests about knowledge, heart, soul and unanswered prayer. Sahih: included by Muslim in his Sahih. The opening protections and the complete final four petitions are in Zayd ibn Arqam’s report.

Sahih Muslim 589b

Component: Fire and grave trials and punishments; wealth, poverty, Dajjal; sin and debt. Sahih: included by Muslim in his Sahih. All these clauses are contained in Aisha’s longer supplication, with order and repeated introductory wording changed.

Sahih Muslim 588a

Component: Trials of life and death. Sahih: included by Muslim in his Sahih. The fourfold refuge after tashahhud includes this clause.

Al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak 1944

Component: Hardness, heedlessness, poverty, humiliation, destitution, unbelief, wickedness, dissension, seeking reputation, ostentation; deafness, muteness, madness, leprosy and serious diseases. Al-Albani, Irwa’ al-Ghalil 3/357: al-Hakim’s chain is on al-Bukhari’s conditions. Al-Hakim’s passage contains the whole middle list and several items omitted by the compilation. The weak Ibn Hibban route discussed in the source is separate from the al-Hakim route graded here.

Sahih al-Bukhari 6369

Component: Anxiety, sorrow, miserliness, heavy debt and being overpowered by others. Sahih: included by al-Bukhari in his Sahih. These phrases occur together in the Anas report.

Sahih al-Bukhari 6365

Component: Being reduced to the feeblest old age and trials of this world. Sahih: included by al-Bukhari in his Sahih. The Sa‘d report includes both clauses.

A compilation assembled from several reports, not one continuous narrated hadith. Every substantive request has a located component source; ordering, linking particles and omissions are editorial. The assessments belong to the individual cited reports and do not authenticate the assembled text as one hadith. Although the original commentary calls this one hadith, the numbered prayer combines clauses from several separately sourced reports.

Closing reflection

From the original edition

Amid the world's idol temples, this is God's ﬁrst House;
We are its guardians, and it is our guardian.

The centre for the acceptance of supplications

Reading note

While making supplications, turn your heart towards Allah and hold the image of the House of Allah firmly in your mind.

ClosingDurood

O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad, the unlettered Prophet, and upon his family, and grant them peace in abundance.

Note from the Urdu edition

Recite Durood at the beginning and end of every manzil. This is a means for supplications to be accepted. (See page 64 of the original edition.)

Reference review

The source’s instruction is retained above. Praise and blessings before duʿā have support in Abu Dawud 1481; the weekly arrangement is the compiler’s. The specific eighty-year reward quoted with Monday’s Durood has not been established as sound. See general references G1 and G3.

General blessings upon the Prophet are supported by Qur’an 33:56. A general encouragement does not by itself establish a particular count, occasion or reward.
